edition: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (IRCC study guide, 2012 text with online updates incl. the current Oath naming King Charles III) – the official guide for tests taken in 2026

exam.rules: Applicants aged 18 to 54 must pass the citizenship knowledge test (in English or French). The test has 20 multiple-choice or true/false questions based only on the official guide Discover Canada; you need at least 15 correct (75%) to pass and have 45 minutes. Applicants get 3 chances to pass. The test checks knowledge of Canada and of the rights and responsibilities of citizenship, not language ability (assessed separately).

sources.title: Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (read online)
sources.note: Official study guide. Facts tested in original wording written by us; no guide text copied.

sources.title: Citizenship test: Study for the test (IRCC)
sources.note: Test format: 20 questions, 15 to pass, 45 minutes, 3 chances; confirms Discover Canada is the guide.

questions.q: In what year was Magna Carta signed in England?
questions.explain: Magna Carta dates from 1215 and is the start of the tradition of ordered liberty that Canada inherited.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Magna Carta)

questions.q: What is another name for Magna Carta?
options: The Charter of the French Language
questions.explain: Magna Carta is also called the Great Charter of Freedoms.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Magna Carta)

questions.q: What is habeas corpus?
options: The right to a trial in French or English
The right to vote in secret
The right to live in any province
The right to challenge unlawful detention by the state
questions.explain: Habeas corpus lets a person challenge being held unlawfully by the state.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

questions.q: Habeas corpus comes from which legal tradition?
questions.explain: The guide states that habeas corpus comes from English common law.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

questions.q: In which year was the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms entrenched in the Constitution?
questions.explain: The Constitution was amended in 1982 to entrench the Charter.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Charter of Rights and Freedoms)

questions.q: According to the opening words of the Charter, Canada is founded on principles that recognize what?
options: Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness
The supremacy of God and the rule of law
questions.explain: The Charter's preamble refers to the supremacy of God and the rule of law.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Charter of Rights and Freedoms)

questions.q: Which of these is a fundamental freedom protected in Canada?
questions.explain: Freedom of peaceful assembly is one of the fundamental freedoms; the others listed are not rights.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

questions.q: Freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression includes which of the following?
options: Freedom of speech and of the press
Freedom to break laws you disagree with
Freedom to avoid military service in wartime
questions.explain: Freedom of expression in Canada includes freedom of speech and freedom of the press.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

questions.q: What do mobility rights allow Canadians to do?
options: Vote in any riding they choose
Move to any country without a visa
Drive without a licence in other provinces
Live and work anywhere in Canada, and enter and leave the country
questions.explain: Mobility rights cover living and working anywhere in Canada, entering and leaving Canada, and applying for a passport.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Mobility rights)

questions.q: Which Charter category protects your freedom to enter and leave Canada?
questions.explain: Entering and leaving Canada freely is part of mobility rights.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Mobility rights)

questions.q: The rights guaranteed in the Charter will not adversely affect which other rights?
options: Treaty and other rights of Aboriginal peoples
Rights of corporations to pay less tax
questions.explain: The Charter states that its guarantees do not adversely affect Aboriginal treaty or other rights.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Aboriginal peoples' rights)

questions.q: Which two languages have equal status in Parliament and throughout the federal government?
questions.explain: English and French are Canada's official languages with equal status in Parliament and federal government.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Official language rights)

questions.q: Which of the following does the guide describe as a fundamental characteristic of Canadian heritage and identity?
questions.explain: Multiculturalism is described as a fundamental characteristic of Canadian heritage and identity.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Multiculturalism)

questions.q: How are men and women treated under Canadian law?
options: They are equal under the law
questions.explain: In Canada, men and women are equal under the law.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Equality of women and men)

questions.q: Which of the following is a crime that is severely punished in Canada?
questions.explain: Forced marriage, spousal abuse, 'honour killings' and female genital mutilation are crimes severely punished under Canadian law.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Equality of women and men)

questions.q: Which of these is one of the sources of Canadian law?
options: Decrees of the Governor General alone
questions.explain: Canadian law draws on laws passed by Parliament and the legislatures, English common law, the French civil code and the unwritten constitution from Great Britain.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

questions.q: Which legal tradition from France is a source of Canadian law?
options: The laws of New France's fur traders
questions.explain: The civil code of France is one source of Canadian law, alongside English common law.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

questions.q: Canada inherited an unwritten constitution from which country?
questions.explain: Part of Canada's constitutional heritage is the unwritten constitution inherited from Great Britain.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

questions.q: What does the 'rule of law' mean?
options: The Prime Minister can overrule the courts
No person or group is above the law
questions.explain: The rule of law, a founding principle in Canada, means everyone, including government, is subject to the law.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Obeying the law)

questions.q: Is serving on a jury in Canada voluntary?
options: No, citizens called to serve are legally required to do so
questions.explain: Citizens who are called for jury duty are legally required to serve.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Serving on a jury)

questions.q: Which of these is a responsibility of Canadian citizenship?
questions.explain: Voting in federal, provincial or territorial and local elections is a responsibility of citizenship.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Citizenship responsibilities)

questions.q: In which elections do Canadians have a responsibility to vote?
options: Federal, provincial or territorial, and local elections
Only elections held in their home country
questions.explain: The right to vote carries a responsibility to vote at all three levels.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Voting)

questions.q: Is military service compulsory in Canada?
options: Yes, for all citizens for one year
No, there is no compulsory military service
questions.explain: Canada has no compulsory military service; serving is a voluntary and honourable choice.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Defending Canada)

questions.q: The regular Canadian Forces are made up of which branches?
options: Air force, police and fire services
questions.explain: The regular Canadian Forces include the navy, army and air force.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Defending Canada)

questions.q: Through which programme can young people learn discipline and responsibility while serving the community?
questions.explain: The guide says young people can learn discipline, responsibility and skills by joining the cadets.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Defending Canada)

questions.q: Besides the Canadian Forces, which is a way to serve Canada mentioned in the guide?
options: Serving in the Coast Guard or local emergency services
Serving as a judge without training
questions.explain: Citizens can also serve in the Coast Guard, police or fire departments.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Defending Canada)

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of taking responsibility for yourself and your family?
options: Getting a job and taking care of your family
questions.explain: Working and caring for one's family are key Canadian values that contribute to dignity and prosperity.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Taking responsibility)

questions.q: Which action helps protect Canada's heritage and environment?
questions.explain: Citizens should avoid waste and pollution and protect natural, cultural and architectural heritage.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Protecting heritage and environment)

questions.q: Which is an example of helping others in the community?
questions.explain: Volunteering, for example at a food bank or helping newcomers, is a way to help others in the community.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship (Helping others)

questions.q: According to the guide, how old is Canada's tradition of ordered liberty?
questions.explain: It traces back to Magna Carta (1215), roughly 800 years ago.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

questions.q: Which freedom allows Canadians to practise any religion or none?
questions.explain: Freedom of conscience and religion is a fundamental freedom.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

questions.q: Which freedom allows Canadians to form or join groups such as unions or clubs?
questions.explain: Freedom of association lets people form and join groups.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

questions.q: Who proclaimed the amended Constitution, including the Charter, in Ottawa in 1982?
questions.explain: Queen Elizabeth II proclaimed the amended Constitution in Ottawa in 1982.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

questions.q: Rights and responsibilities in Canada are secured by what?
questions.explain: Canadian citizens' rights and responsibilities come from history and are secured by Canadian law.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship

questions.q: What are the three founding peoples of Canada?
questions.explain: Canada's three founding peoples are Aboriginal, French and British.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are

questions.q: The phrase 'Peace, Order and Good Government' comes from which document?
options: The Charter of Rights and Freedoms
questions.explain: The phrase comes from the British North America Act of 1867.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are

questions.q: According to Discover Canada, Canada is the only country in North America that is a what?
questions.explain: Canada is North America's only constitutional monarchy.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are

questions.q: Which document first guaranteed Aboriginal territorial rights?
questions.explain: The Royal Proclamation of 1763 by King George III first guaranteed Aboriginal territorial rights.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Aboriginal peoples)

questions.q: Which king issued the Royal Proclamation of 1763?
questions.explain: King George III issued the Royal Proclamation of 1763.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Aboriginal peoples)

questions.q: What was the purpose of residential schools?
options: To educate immigrant children in French
To assimilate Aboriginal children into mainstream culture
To train teachers for the North
questions.explain: Residential schools aimed to assimilate Aboriginal children; their languages and cultural practices were mostly prohibited.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Aboriginal peoples)

questions.q: In what year did the federal government formally apologize to former students of residential schools?
questions.explain: Ottawa formally apologized to former residential school students in 2008.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Aboriginal peoples)

questions.q: Residential schools operated from the 1800s until approximately when?
questions.explain: Residential schools existed from the 1800s until the 1980s.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Aboriginal peoples)

questions.q: The term 'Aboriginal peoples' refers to which three distinct groups?
questions.explain: Aboriginal peoples comprise First Nations (Indian), Inuit and Métis.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Aboriginal peoples)

questions.q: When did the term 'First Nations' come into use?
questions.explain: The term First Nations began to be used in the 1970s.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (First Nations)

questions.q: About half of First Nations people live on reserve land in roughly how many communities?
questions.explain: Roughly half of First Nations people live on reserve land in about 600 communities.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (First Nations)

questions.q: What does the word 'Inuit' mean in Inuktitut?
questions.explain: Inuit means 'the people' in Inuktitut. ('Our land' is the meaning of Nunavut.)
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Inuit)

questions.q: Who are the Métis?
options: Loyalists who came from the United States
A distinct people of mixed Aboriginal and European ancestry
Descendants of French settlers in Acadia
questions.explain: The Métis are a distinct people of mixed Aboriginal and European ancestry.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Métis)

questions.q: Where do most Métis live?
questions.explain: The majority of Métis live in the Prairie provinces.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Métis)

questions.q: What is the name of the Métis language?
questions.explain: The Métis have their own distinct language, Michif.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Métis)

questions.q: About what percentage of Aboriginal people are First Nations?
questions.explain: About 65% are First Nations, 30% Métis and 4% Inuit.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Aboriginal peoples)

questions.q: Which is the smallest of the three Aboriginal groups by population?
options: They are all equal in size
questions.explain: Inuit make up about 4% of Aboriginal people, the smallest share.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Aboriginal peoples)

questions.q: By law, the federal government must provide services throughout Canada in which languages?
questions.explain: Federal services must be available in both official languages across Canada.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (English and French)

questions.q: Which is the only officially bilingual province?
questions.explain: New Brunswick is Canada's only officially bilingual province.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (English and French)

questions.q: Who are the Acadians?
options: Métis people of the Red River
Descendants of French colonists who settled the Maritimes from 1604
Descendants of the United Empire Loyalists
questions.explain: Acadians descend from French colonists who began settling the Maritimes in 1604.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Acadians)

questions.q: What is the deportation of the Acadians from 1755 to 1763 called?
questions.explain: The deportation of more than two-thirds of Acadians is known as the Great Upheaval.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Acadians)

questions.q: During the Great Upheaval, about what share of Acadians were deported?
questions.explain: More than two-thirds of the Acadians were deported between 1755 and 1763.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Acadians)

questions.q: Most Quebecers are descendants of about how many French settlers from the 1600s and 1700s?
questions.explain: Most Quebecers descend from about 8,500 French settlers.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Quebecers)

questions.q: In 2006, what did the House of Commons recognize?
options: That Quebec is an independent country
That the Québécois form a nation within a united Canada
That French is the only official language of Canada
questions.explain: In 2006 the House of Commons recognized that the Québécois form a nation within a united Canada.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Quebecers)

questions.q: Since the 1970s, where have most immigrants to Canada come from?
questions.explain: Most immigrants since the 1970s have come from Asian countries.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Diversity in Canada)

questions.q: According to Discover Canada, what is the largest religious affiliation in Canada?
questions.explain: Catholics are the largest religious group, followed by Protestant churches.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Religion)

questions.q: How do the great majority of Canadians identify their religion?
questions.explain: The great majority of Canadians identify as Christians.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Religion)

questions.q: How are gay and lesbian Canadians treated under the law?
options: Their rights differ in each riding
They have full equal protection, including access to civil marriage
questions.explain: Gay and lesbian Canadians enjoy full legal protection and equal treatment, including civil marriage.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Diversity)

questions.q: Who was John Buchan, Lord Tweedsmuir?
options: The first Prime Minister of Canada
A Father of Confederation from Quebec
A Governor General who encouraged immigrants to keep their identity while contributing to Canada
The founder of the Hudson's Bay Company
questions.explain: John Buchan (Lord Tweedsmuir) was Governor General from 1935 to 1940 and spoke about unity in diversity.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Unity in diversity)

questions.q: Where were most Canadians born?
questions.explain: Most Canadians have been born in Canada, as has been true since the 1800s.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Diversity in Canada)

questions.q: Canada has the oldest continuous tradition of what kind in the world?
questions.explain: Canada has the oldest continuous constitutional tradition in the world.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are

questions.q: English-speaking Canada was shaped by settlers from which countries?
questions.explain: Hundreds of thousands of English, Welsh, Scottish and Irish settlers shaped English-speaking Canada.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (English-speaking Canada)

questions.q: In two of Canada's largest cities, which languages are the second most spoken at home after English?
questions.explain: Chinese languages are the second most spoken at home in two of Canada's largest cities.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Diversity in Canada)

questions.q: Where do most Francophones in Canada live?
questions.explain: Most Francophones live in Quebec; about one million live in Ontario, New Brunswick and Manitoba.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (English and French)

questions.q: What are newcomers to Canada expected to do?
options: Keep violent or hateful prejudices from their past
Embrace democratic principles such as the rule of law
questions.explain: Newcomers are expected to embrace democratic principles and not bring violent, extreme or hateful prejudices.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Becoming Canadian)

questions.q: Where are the ancestors of Aboriginal peoples believed to have migrated from many thousands of years ago?
questions.explain: Aboriginal ancestors are believed to have migrated from Asia many thousands of years ago.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Aboriginal peoples)

questions.q: Where are Aboriginal and treaty rights protected?
questions.explain: Aboriginal and treaty rights are set out in the Canadian Constitution.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Aboriginal peoples)

questions.q: Canadian society largely grew out of which two European civilizations brought by settlers?
questions.explain: Canada largely developed from English-speaking and French-speaking Christian civilizations brought by settlers.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (English and French)

questions.q: Canada is often called a 'land of immigrants' because:
options: Millions of newcomers helped build and defend the country over the past 200 years
Immigration is the only source of population growth
questions.explain: Millions of newcomers over 200 years helped build and defend Canada, though most Canadians are born in Canada.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Who We Are (Diversity in Canada)

questions.q: Why did European explorers call Aboriginal people 'Indians'?
options: It came from the name of a river
It was the word Aboriginal people used for themselves
It was a title given by the King of France
They believed they had reached the East Indies
questions.explain: Early explorers thought they had arrived in the East Indies.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Aboriginal peoples)

questions.q: Which Aboriginal peoples were farmers and hunters?
questions.explain: The Huron-Wendat and Iroquois of the Great Lakes region farmed and hunted.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Aboriginal peoples)

questions.q: Which Aboriginal people were nomadic and followed the bison herds?
questions.explain: The Sioux followed the bison herds on the Prairies.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Aboriginal peoples)

questions.q: What caused many Aboriginal deaths after contact with Europeans?
options: European diseases to which they had no immunity
questions.explain: Large numbers of Aboriginal people died from European diseases.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Aboriginal peoples)

questions.q: Who were the first Europeans to reach Canada, about 1,000 years ago?
questions.explain: Vikings from Iceland, who had colonized Greenland, reached Labrador and Newfoundland.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (The first Europeans)

questions.q: Where can the remains of a Viking settlement, now a World Heritage site, be found?
questions.explain: The Viking settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (The first Europeans)

questions.q: In 1497, who was the first explorer to draw a map of Canada's East Coast?
questions.explain: John Cabot, an Italian sailing for England, mapped the East Coast in 1497.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (The first Europeans)

questions.q: For which country was John Cabot sailing when he reached Canada in 1497?
questions.explain: Cabot was Italian but sailed in the service of England.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (The first Europeans)

questions.q: Between 1534 and 1542, Jacques Cartier claimed land for which king?
questions.explain: Cartier made three voyages and claimed the land for King Francis I of France.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Exploring a river, naming Canada)

questions.q: The name 'Canada' comes from the Iroquoian word 'kanata'. What does it mean?
questions.explain: Kanata means 'village' in the Iroquoian language.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Exploring a river, naming Canada)

questions.q: Who was the first European to explore the St. Lawrence River and see the sites of Québec City and Montreal?
questions.explain: Jacques Cartier was the first European to explore the St. Lawrence.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Royal New France)

questions.q: In 1604, Pierre de Monts and Samuel de Champlain founded the first European settlement north of Florida. Where was it first established?
options: St. Croix Island, then Port-Royal in Acadia
questions.explain: The settlement began on St. Croix Island and then moved to Port-Royal in Acadia (present-day Nova Scotia).
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Royal New France)

questions.q: In what year did Samuel de Champlain build a fortress at what is now Québec City?
questions.explain: Champlain founded Québec City in 1608.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Royal New France)

questions.q: Champlain allied with the Algonquin, Montagnais and Huron against which group?
questions.explain: Champlain's allies fought the Iroquois Confederacy; the French and Iroquois made peace in 1701.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Royal New France)

questions.q: In what year did the French and the Iroquois make peace?
questions.explain: After a century of conflict, the French and Iroquois made peace in 1701.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Royal New France)

questions.q: Which animal's pelts drove the early fur trade?
questions.explain: European demand for beaver pelts drove the fur trade.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Royal New France)

questions.q: Who received exclusive trading rights over the Hudson Bay watershed in 1670?
questions.explain: King Charles II granted the Hudson's Bay Company exclusive trading rights in 1670.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Struggle for a continent)

questions.q: Which king granted the Hudson's Bay Company its trading rights in 1670?
questions.explain: King Charles II granted the Company its charter in 1670.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Struggle for a continent)

questions.q: What were voyageurs and coureurs des bois known for?
options: Travelling by canoe in the fur trade
questions.explain: These skilled canoeists were part of the fur trade economy and formed alliances with First Nations.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Struggle for a continent)

questions.q: In 1759, which battle ended France's empire in America?
options: The Battle of the Plains of Abraham
questions.explain: The British defeated the French at the Plains of Abraham at Québec City in 1759.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Struggle for a continent)

questions.q: Which two commanders were killed at the Battle of the Plains of Abraham?
options: James Wolfe and the Marquis de Montcalm
questions.explain: Both Brigadier James Wolfe and the Marquis de Montcalm died in the battle.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Struggle for a continent)

questions.q: What were French-speaking Catholics in the Province of Quebec called after the British conquest?
questions.explain: They were known as habitants or Canadiens.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (The Province of Quebec)

questions.q: What did the Quebec Act of 1774 allow?
options: The end of the fur trade
Free trade with the United States
Religious freedom for Catholics and the right to hold public office
questions.explain: The Quebec Act let Catholics practise their religion and hold public office, and restored French civil law.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (A tradition of accommodation)

questions.q: Under the Quebec Act of 1774, which legal system was used for civil matters?
questions.explain: The Quebec Act restored French civil law while keeping British criminal law.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (A tradition of accommodation)

questions.q: Who were the United Empire Loyalists?
options: People who stayed loyal to the Crown and left the American colonies for Canada
Soldiers who fought in the Boer War
questions.explain: After the American colonies declared independence in 1776, more than 40,000 Loyalists moved to Nova Scotia and Quebec.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (United Empire Loyalists)

questions.q: About how many Loyalists fled to Nova Scotia and Quebec after the American Revolution?
questions.explain: More than 40,000 Loyalists came north.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (United Empire Loyalists)

questions.q: Who led thousands of Mohawk Loyalists into Canada?
questions.explain: Joseph Brant led thousands of Mohawk Loyalists into Canada.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (United Empire Loyalists)

questions.q: In 1792, some Black Nova Scotians moved to which British colony for freed slaves?
questions.explain: Some Black Loyalists left Nova Scotia for Freetown, Sierra Leone, in 1792.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (United Empire Loyalists)

questions.q: Where was the first representative assembly in what is now Canada elected, in 1758?
questions.explain: The first representative assembly was elected in Halifax in 1758.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (The beginnings of democracy)

questions.q: What did the Constitutional Act of 1791 do?
options: Divided the Province of Quebec into Upper Canada and Lower Canada
questions.explain: The Constitutional Act of 1791 created Upper Canada and Lower Canada and their first elected assemblies.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (The beginnings of democracy)

questions.q: Upper Canada later became which province?
questions.explain: Upper Canada became Ontario; Lower Canada became Quebec.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (The beginnings of democracy)

questions.q: Lower Canada later became which province?
questions.explain: Lower Canada was mainly French-speaking and Catholic, and became Quebec.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (The beginnings of democracy)

questions.q: In which year did the name 'Canada' first become official, with the Constitutional Act?
questions.explain: The name Canada became official with the Constitutional Act of 1791.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (The beginnings of democracy)

questions.q: What was the collective name for the Atlantic colonies and the two Canadas before Confederation?
questions.explain: Together they were known as British North America.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (The beginnings of democracy)

questions.q: Which was the first province in the British Empire to move toward abolishing slavery, in 1793?
questions.explain: Upper Canada, under Lieutenant Governor John Graves Simcoe, moved to abolish slavery in 1793.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Abolition of slavery)

questions.q: Who was the Lieutenant Governor of Upper Canada who led the first move to abolish slavery?
questions.explain: John Graves Simcoe led Upper Canada's 1793 move against slavery.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Abolition of slavery)

questions.q: In what year was slavery abolished throughout the British Empire?
questions.explain: The British Parliament abolished slavery throughout the Empire in 1833 (it banned the slave trade in 1807).
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Abolition of slavery)

questions.q: What was the Underground Railroad?
options: A secret military supply route in 1812
A network that helped slaves escape from the United States to Canada
questions.explain: The Underground Railroad was an anti-slavery network that helped thousands of slaves escape to Canada.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (Abolition of slavery)

questions.q: In what year did the Montreal Stock Exchange open?
questions.explain: The Montreal Stock Exchange opened in 1832.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (A growing economy)

questions.q: For many years, Canada's economy was based mainly on what?
options: Farming and exporting natural resources such as fur, fish and timber
questions.explain: For centuries the economy relied on farming and natural resource exports.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (A growing economy)

questions.q: Which Hudson's Bay Company post later became the city of Winnipeg?
questions.explain: Fort Garry grew into Winnipeg.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (A growing economy)

questions.q: In what year did the United States invade Canada, starting the War of 1812?
questions.explain: American forces invaded Canada in June 1812 and were defeated.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (The War of 1812)

questions.q: Which Shawnee chief helped defend Canada in the War of 1812?
questions.explain: Chief Tecumseh led the Shawnee in support of the defence of Canada.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canada's History (The War of 1812)

questions.q: Which British general captured Detroit in 1812 and was later killed at Queenston Heights?

questions.q: Which level of government is responsible for health and natural resources?
questions.explain: Health and natural resources are provincial responsibilities.

questions.q: What are the three parts of Parliament?
options: The House of Commons, the provinces and the territories
The Sovereign, the Senate and the House of Commons
The Governor General, the Supreme Court and the Senate
The Prime Minister, the Cabinet and the courts

questions.explain: Senators serve until age 75.

options: It must be signed by the Prime Minister only
It must be approved in a national referendum
It must be approved by every province
It must pass both chambers and receive royal assent

questions.q: Who gives royal assent to bills on behalf of the Sovereign?
questions.explain: The Governor General grants royal assent on behalf of the Sovereign.

questions.explain: At second reading, members debate the principle of the bill.

questions.q: At which stage is a bill studied clause by clause?
questions.explain: At committee stage, members study the bill clause by clause.

questions.q: What happens at first reading of a bill?

It is considered read for the first time and printed
It is sent to the Supreme Court

questions.q: At which stage of a bill can members make further amendments after committee study?
questions.explain: At report stage, members can make other amendments.

questions.q: Who is Canada's Head of State?
options: The Sovereign (King Charles III as of October 2026)

questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Constitutional monarchy)

questions.q: Who is the head of government in Canada?
questions.explain: The Prime Minister is head of government; the Sovereign is Head of State.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Constitutional monarchy)

questions.q: Who represents the Sovereign in Canada?
options: The Speaker of the House of Commons
questions.explain: The Governor General represents the Sovereign in Canada.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Constitutional monarchy)

questions.q: How is the Governor General appointed?
options: By the Sovereign on the advice of the Prime Minister
questions.explain: The Sovereign appoints the Governor General on the Prime Minister's advice, usually for five years.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Constitutional monarchy)

questions.q: For how long is the Governor General usually appointed?
questions.explain: The Governor General usually serves five years.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Constitutional monarchy)

questions.q: Who represents the Sovereign in each of the ten provinces?
options: The mayor of the capital city
questions.explain: A Lieutenant Governor represents the Sovereign in each province.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Constitutional monarchy)

questions.q: Who appoints the Lieutenant Governors?
options: The Governor General, on the advice of the Prime Minister
questions.explain: The Governor General appoints Lieutenant Governors on the Prime Minister's advice.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Constitutional monarchy)

questions.q: Who represents the federal government in each of the three territories?
questions.explain: Each territory has a Commissioner who represents the federal government.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Constitutional monarchy)

questions.q: In a province, whose role is similar to that of the Prime Minister?
questions.explain: The Premier plays a role like the Prime Minister's at the provincial level.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Constitutional monarchy)

questions.q: What are the three branches of government in Canada?
options: Senate, House of Commons and Cabinet
questions.explain: The three branches are executive, legislative and judicial.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Constitutional monarchy)

questions.q: Which of these titles is used for members of provincial or territorial legislatures?
questions.explain: Depending on the province or territory, members are called MLAs, MNAs, MPPs or MHAs.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Constitutional monarchy)

questions.q: What happens if the Cabinet loses a non-confidence vote in the House of Commons?
options: The Supreme Court appoints a new government
questions.explain: Ministers must keep the confidence of the House and resign if they lose a non-confidence vote.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Parliamentary democracy)

questions.q: Who selects the Cabinet ministers?
questions.explain: The Prime Minister selects Cabinet ministers.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Parliamentary democracy)

questions.q: The House of Commons is made up of whom?
options: Members of Parliament elected by the people
questions.explain: The House of Commons is the representative chamber of elected MPs.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Parliamentary democracy)

questions.q: What does a provincial legislature consist of?
options: The Governor General and the House of Commons
The Lieutenant Governor and the elected Assembly
questions.explain: Provincial legislatures comprise the Lieutenant Governor and the elected Assembly.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Parliamentary democracy)

questions.q: Which of these countries is also a constitutional monarchy?
questions.explain: The guide lists Australia among other constitutional monarchies.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Constitutional monarchy)

questions.q: As Head of the Commonwealth, the Sovereign links Canada to which group?
options: The member states of the European Union
questions.explain: The Sovereign is Head of the Commonwealth, linking Canada to other member nations.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Constitutional monarchy)

questions.q: Why does federalism allow provinces to adopt different policies?
options: So they can tailor policies to the needs of their own populations
Because only the Senate makes laws
Because the Constitution has no rules
questions.explain: Federalism lets provinces tailor policies to their populations.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Federal state)

questions.q: Why do the territories not have provincial status?
options: They are owned by the Crown
They are part of the United States
questions.explain: The three territories have small populations and are not provinces, though their governments perform similar functions.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Federal state)

questions.q: What does the Sovereign symbolize in Canada?
options: Canadian sovereignty and the focus of citizenship and allegiance
questions.explain: The Sovereign is a non-partisan symbol of sovereignty and the focus of allegiance.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Constitutional monarchy)

questions.q: What do new citizens promise in the Oath of Citizenship?
options: To vote for the governing party
To give up all other languages
Allegiance to the King, to observe the laws including the Constitution, and to fulfil their duties as citizens

questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Oath of Citizenship

questions.q: The current Oath of Citizenship recognizes the Constitution's protection of which rights?
options: Rights of foreign residents to vote
Aboriginal and treaty rights of First Nations, Inuit and Métis
Rights of provinces to leave Canada
questions.explain: The oath now refers to the Aboriginal and treaty rights of First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Oath of Citizenship

questions.q: In Canada, to whom do new citizens pledge their loyalty?
options: The Sovereign, who represents all Canadians
questions.explain: Canadians pledge allegiance to a person, the Sovereign, who embodies the country, rather than to a document or flag.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Oath of Citizenship

questions.q: Who has the responsibility and right to vote in Canada?
questions.explain: Citizens 18 or older can vote in federal, provincial/territorial and municipal elections.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Making laws)

questions.q: How often are members of the House of Commons traditionally elected?
questions.explain: MPs are traditionally elected every four years.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – How Canadians Govern Themselves (Parliamentary democracy)

questions.q: Under current legislation, when are federal elections held?
options: On the third Monday in October every four years after the last election
On the first Tuesday in November every four years
questions.explain: Fixed-date legislation sets federal elections on the third Monday in October, four years after the last general election.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections

questions.q: Who can ask the Governor General to call an election earlier than the fixed date?
questions.explain: The Prime Minister may advise the Governor General to call an earlier election.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections

questions.q: What is another name for a federal electoral district?
questions.explain: Electoral districts are also called ridings or constituencies.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections

questions.q: How many Members of Parliament does each electoral district elect?
questions.explain: Each electoral district elects one MP.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections

questions.q: Who can be a candidate in a federal election?
options: Only members of a political party
A Canadian citizen aged 18 or older
questions.explain: Citizens 18 or older may run in a federal election.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections

questions.q: Which candidate becomes the MP for an electoral district?
options: The candidate with more than 75% of votes
The candidate chosen by the Prime Minister
The candidate with the most votes
questions.explain: The candidate with the most votes in the riding becomes its MP.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections

questions.q: What are the requirements to vote in a federal election?
options: Be a permanent resident and pay taxes
Be a member of a political party
Be a Canadian citizen, at least 18 on election day, and on the voters' list
Be at least 21 and own property
questions.explain: You must be a citizen, 18 or older on voting day, and registered on the voters' list.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (Voting)

questions.q: Which neutral agency of Parliament runs federal elections and prepares voters' lists?
questions.explain: Elections Canada produces voters' lists from the National Register of Electors.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (Voting)

questions.q: What is the National Register of Electors?
options: A permanent database of Canadians 18 or older who are qualified to vote
A list of Members of Parliament
A list of all political parties
questions.explain: The National Register is a permanent database of qualified electors.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (Voting)

questions.q: What does the voter information card tell you?
questions.explain: The card mailed by Elections Canada shows when and where to vote.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (Voting)

questions.q: If you did not receive a voter information card, can you still be added to the voters' list on election day?
options: Yes, you can be added at any time, including on election day
Only if you pay a fee
questions.explain: You can be added to the voters' list at any time, including election day.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (Voting)

questions.q: What does a secret ballot guarantee?
options: Only your family may know your vote
No one can see how you voted or force you to reveal it
Your employer can check your vote
questions.explain: The law guarantees a secret ballot; no one, including family or employer, can require you to reveal your vote.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (Secret ballot)

questions.q: If you cannot vote on election day, what can you do?
options: Send your vote to your MP by email
Ask a friend to vote twice
Vote at an advance poll or by special ballot
questions.explain: Advance polls and special ballots are available if you cannot vote on election day.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (Voting procedures)

questions.q: How do you mark a federal ballot?
options: Put an X in the circle next to the candidate of your choice
Sign your name beside the candidate
questions.explain: Mark an X in the circle beside your chosen candidate.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (Voting procedures)

questions.q: After an election, who is usually invited by the Governor General to form the government?
options: The leader of the party with the most senators
The leader of the party with the most seats in the House of Commons
questions.explain: The Governor General normally invites the leader of the party with the most seats.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (After an election)

questions.q: What is a majority government?
options: When the governing party wins every seat
When the governing party holds at least half of the seats in the House of Commons
When the Senate controls the government
When two parties share power equally
questions.explain: A majority government holds at least half the seats.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (After an election)

questions.q: What is a minority government?
options: When the governing party holds fewer than half of the seats in the House of Commons
When an independent becomes Prime Minister
When the Senate has more members than the House
When the government has no Cabinet
questions.explain: A minority government holds less than half the seats.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (After an election)

questions.q: Which of the following is usually a matter of confidence?
options: A private member's motion about a holiday
questions.explain: Votes on major issues such as the budget are matters of confidence.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (After an election)

questions.q: If the government is defeated in a confidence vote, what usually happens?
options: The Senate chooses a new Prime Minister
The Prime Minister asks the Governor General to call an election
questions.explain: When defeated on a confidence matter, the Prime Minister usually asks the Governor General to call an election.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (After an election)

questions.q: Who makes up the Cabinet?
options: The Governor General and the Lieutenant Governors
The Prime Minister and the ministers
questions.explain: The Prime Minister and the Cabinet ministers form the Cabinet.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (After an election)

questions.q: What are some responsibilities of the Cabinet?
options: Preparing the budget and proposing most new laws
Appointing judges to provincial courts only
questions.explain: The Cabinet makes important decisions, prepares the budget and proposes most new laws.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (After an election)

questions.q: What is the Official Opposition?
options: The party with the fewest seats
The opposition party with the most members in the House of Commons
questions.explain: The opposition party with the most seats is the Official Opposition, or His Majesty's Loyal Opposition (the guide's 2012 text says 'Her Majesty's').
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (After an election)

questions.q: What is the role of opposition parties?
options: To peacefully oppose or try to improve government proposals
questions.explain: Opposition parties peacefully oppose or try to improve government proposals.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (After an election)

questions.q: Who usually heads a municipal government?
questions.explain: Municipal councils are usually led by a mayor (or reeve) with councillors or aldermen.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (Other levels of government)

questions.q: What are the laws passed by municipal governments called?
questions.explain: Municipal governments pass by-laws that affect only the local community.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (Other levels of government)

questions.q: Which of these is usually a municipal responsibility?
questions.explain: Municipalities handle services such as snow removal, firefighting and local transit.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (Other levels of government)

questions.q: Who leads First Nations bands?
questions.explain: First Nations have band chiefs and councillors with responsibilities on reserves.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (First Nations)

questions.q: Which responsibilities do First Nations band councils have on reserves?
questions.explain: Band councils have major responsibilities on reserves, including housing and schools.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (First Nations)

questions.q: Who are the elected officials at the federal level?
questions.explain: Federal elected officials are MPs.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (Levels of government)

questions.q: When are election results counted?
options: At the end of the year
questions.explain: Officials count ballots right after polls close; results are then made public.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (Secret ballot)

questions.q: Who runs federal government departments?
questions.explain: Cabinet ministers are responsible for running federal departments.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (After an election)

questions.q: Do provincial and municipal elections follow exactly the same rules as federal elections?
options: There are no rules for provincial elections
Municipal elections have no secret ballot
No; they also use a secret ballot but their rules differ
questions.explain: Provincial, territorial and municipal elections use secret ballots but have different rules.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (Other levels of government)

questions.q: Can someone require you to tell them how you voted?
options: No, not even a family member, employer or union representative
questions.explain: You may discuss your vote, but no one can require you to disclose it.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Federal Elections (Secret ballot)

questions.q: What does 'presumption of innocence' mean?
options: Everyone is innocent until proven guilty
Everyone is guilty until proven innocent

questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Justice System

questions.q: What does 'due process' mean?
options: Trials must be completed within a week
Police may search any home without reason
The government must respect all the legal rights a person is entitled to
Only citizens may go to court
questions.explain: Due process means the government must respect a person's legal rights.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Justice System

questions.q: What is the highest court in Canada?
options: The Court of Appeal of Ontario
questions.explain: The Supreme Court of Canada is the highest court.

questions.q: Which court deals with matters concerning the federal government?
questions.explain: The Federal Court of Canada handles matters concerning the federal government.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Justice System (Courts)

questions.q: Which court hears civil cases involving small sums of money?
questions.explain: Small claims courts hear civil cases involving small amounts of money.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Justice System (Courts)

questions.q: Which provinces have their own provincial police forces?
options: Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island
questions.explain: Ontario and Quebec have provincial police forces.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Justice System (Police)

questions.q: What role does the RCMP play in most provinces and territories?

questions.q: Which police force enforces federal laws throughout Canada?
questions.explain: The RCMP enforces federal laws across Canada.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Justice System (Police)

questions.q: If you cannot afford a lawyer, what can you do?
options: Seek legal aid, which is free or low-cost in most communities
Ask the police to be your lawyer
Represent yourself only in the Supreme Court
questions.explain: Most communities offer legal aid at no or low cost.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Justice System (Getting legal help)

questions.q: Can you question the police about their service or conduct?
options: Yes; almost all police forces have a process for raising concerns
Only through a Member of Parliament
Only if you are a lawyer
questions.explain: You can question police conduct; nearly all forces have a complaints process.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Justice System (Police)

questions.q: To whom does the law in Canada apply?
options: Everyone, including judges, politicians and police
questions.explain: The law applies to everyone, including judges, politicians and police.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Justice System (Laws)

questions.q: In Canada, who makes the laws?
questions.explain: Elected representatives make laws, courts settle disputes and police enforce laws.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Justice System (Laws)

questions.q: What is the role of the police?
options: To keep people safe and enforce the law
questions.explain: Police keep people safe and enforce the law; courts decide guilt.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Justice System (Police)

questions.q: What does the blindfolded Lady Justice represent?
options: Impartiality: judging only on the facts
questions.explain: The blindfold symbolizes impartiality, judging only by the facts.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Justice System

questions.q: Which of these is a situation in which you can ask the police for help?
options: If you want to start a business
If you want to change your vote
questions.explain: Police can help with accidents, theft, assault, witnessing a crime or a missing person.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Justice System (Police)

questions.q: Which level of court usually deals with lesser offences?
questions.explain: Provincial courts try most lesser offences.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Justice System (Courts)

questions.q: What role do laws play in Canadian society?
options: They allow police to ignore rights
They provide order and a peaceful way to settle disputes
questions.explain: Laws provide order, settle disputes peacefully and express Canadian values.

questions.q: Who settles disputes under Canadian law?
questions.explain: Courts settle disputes; police enforce laws.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – The Justice System (Laws)

questions.q: Who proclaimed red and white as Canada's national colours in 1921?

questions.q: What is Canada's official Royal Flag?

questions.q: Which flag served as Canada's national flag for about 100 years before 1965?

questions.q: What is Canada's best-known symbol?

questions.q: The maple leaf is carved on the headstones of whom?
options: Canadian soldiers who died in war
questions.explain: The maple leaf appears on headstones of fallen Canadian soldiers.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canadian Symbols (The maple leaf)

questions.q: Which symbol was used by French royalty for over a thousand years?

questions.q: In what year did Quebec adopt its own flag based on the cross and the fleur-de-lys?

questions.q: What is Canada's national motto?
options: A Mari Usque Ad Mare (From sea to sea)
questions.explain: Canada's motto, A Mari Usque Ad Mare, means 'from sea to sea'.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canadian Symbols (Coat of arms and motto)

questions.q: When did Canada adopt an official coat of arms and national motto?

questions.q: The Peace Tower was completed in 1927 in memory of what?

questions.q: What do the Books of Remembrance in the Peace Tower contain?
options: The names of all Prime Ministers
The names of those who died serving Canada in wars or on duty

questions.q: What is Canada's national winter sport?

questions.q: Which sport has the most registered players in Canada?
questions.explain: Soccer has the most registered players of any game in Canada.

questions.q: Which sport was introduced to Canada by Scottish pioneers?
questions.explain: Curling was brought by Scottish pioneers.

questions.q: Which is the second most popular sport in Canada, according to the guide?
questions.explain: Canadian football is the second most popular sport.

questions.q: The beaver was adopted as a symbol centuries ago by which organization?
questions.explain: The beaver was a symbol of the Hudson's Bay Company.

questions.q: On which Canadian coin does the beaver appear?

questions.q: Which of these is an objective of the Official Languages Act?

Establishing equality between French and English in Parliament and the federal government
Making English the only language of work
questions.explain: The Act aims for equality of English and French in federal institutions and support for minority language communities.
questions.ref: Discover Canada – Canadian Symbols (Official languages)

questions.q: In what year was 'O Canada' proclaimed as the national anthem?

questions.q: Where was 'O Canada' first sung, in 1880?
questions.explain: O Canada was first sung in Québec City in 1880.
